The US manufacturing recovery is accelerating:

ISM Manufacturing PMI rose +2.3 points in July, to 55.6, the highest since May 2022.

This marks the 7th consecutive monthly expansion.

Since December 2025, the index has surged +7.7 points, the biggest increase since the 2020 pandemic recovery.

This comes as new orders rose +0.7 points, to 56.7, the 3rd-highest since February 2022, pointing to further strength ahead.

At the same time, the employment index jumped +3.1 points, to 52.8, the highest since August 2022, marking the first monthly expansion since January 2025.

Meanwhile, prices paid fell -1.9 points, to 71.1, the lowest since February, posting the 3rd consecutive monthly decline by a total of -13.5 points. 

Manufacturing activity is gaining momentum.

BREAKING: US job openings dropped -178,000 in June, to 7.36 million, the lowest since March.

This marks the 2nd consecutive monthly decline, bringing the total drop to -226,000.

The decline was driven by private education and health services, as well as leisure and hospitality, which fell -133,000 and -86,000, respectively.

This was followed by wholesale trade and professional and business services, which declined -74,000 and -71,000, respectively.

Despite the decline, there are still 265,000 more available vacancies than unemployed workers, the 2nd-largest difference since January 2025.

As a result, the ratio of job openings to unemployed workers remains at 1.0, the highest since January 2025.

The labor market is becoming increasingly unstable.

$TLN, one of PJM's largest power producers, raised its 2028 free cash flow outlook by 11% today, from $36 to $40/share, as PJM power and capacity prices continue to strengthen.

>70% of PJM's 10 highest peak-demand days since 2013 have occurred in the last 15 months. Five were in July alone.

Key quote:
"We were discussing transacting long-term PPAs with hyperscalers at prices in the $80/MWh range. And now the forward wholesale prices for capacity and energy are approaching those levels, if not exceeding them." 

>So Talen can increasingly choose to hedge power in the merchant market instead of committing it to a hyperscaler for 15–20 years. Prospective customers will now have to pay more to persuade Talen to lock up that supply.

>There is also more visibility than in a typical merchant power cycle. Hyperscalers are already signing long-term leases today for data-center capacity scheduled to begin operating in 2028.

>At roughly a $15B market cap, Talen's base 2028 outlook implies about $1.9B of adjusted free cash flow, or just over 8x FCF.

>On top of this, management  expects to return at least 70% of cumulative free cash flow to shareholders through buybacks, which is not in the guidance.

>If the stock stays near today's price, that's enough to retire roughly one-fifth of the company, putting the stock on ~6.5x FCF. 

>The market clearly expects today's merchant pricing to fade. If it doesn't, this valuation is hard to square.

Stock only +3% on these numbers AH. 

What am I missing?

tweets.text:
The liquidity debate is becoming less about a single “debt maturity wall” and more about the number of claims competing for capital.

Over the past five years, US public debt grew 6.8% a year. Global liquidity rose just 2.2% pa, while my US net liquidity proxy contracted by 3.0% pa.

That does not prove a funding shortage. Debt and liquidity do not need to grow at the same rate.

But the direction matters. Governments are refinancing more debt and running persistent deficits, while the AI build-out is also driving heavy corporate borrowing and capital spending.

More high-quality claims are competing for investor demand, dealer balance sheets and funding capacity into a 6-month global liquidity slowdown (Liquidity aggregates up but momentum down). 

Markets are absorbing it, but the risk is that this growing financing burden becomes much harder to manage if yields rise further. Bessent blinked last week and helped weaken the dollar (via the JPY) - liquidity positive. The MOVE index seems to be 'managed' well. Credit has started to widen, but hasn't broken out. So signs of stress arent there but the conditions are forming. 

Real Rates could be the tell - and they have broken out. Historically not good for risk assets as they have portended increased volatility & downside moves.

thread_tweets.full_text: @SugarRayRob2 @AllVentured @ElClutch AI sales is not the same as cloud sales. For both AWS and Microsoft, frontier model cloud sales are under 10%. And when OpenAI and Anthropic go to zero, some other open source LLM will simply take their place in compute usage.

thread_tweets.text:
Both Microsoft and AWS report frontier model use of their cloud services. Their non-frontier usage is 90%+. 

But think about it another way. Let's say we both agree that OpenAI and Anthropic are going to zero. What will replace them? Nothing? Or will they be replaced by cheaper open source models that still require... compute. 

If you believe that AI technology is valid, then someone will have to provide the user's with an LLM. And then that someone will have to rent datacenter space. 

I am 100% aligned with the view that frontier models are cooked, as the kids would say. But if the underlying technology is real, it does not matter how much of cloud services are being used by frontier models. 

That is like asking, back in 1997, how much of the internet browsing is being done by Netscape. Who cares? Netscape was replaced by someone else. 

Now, if you think that AI is snake oil, then that is a different argument. But I don't need frontier models for the datacenter story to be valid. If anything, frontier models dying could be the best thing for AI and thus compute demand.

thread_tweets.text:
Models run on datacenters. You cannot have AI without cloud computing. So your first sentence is kind of all I need, from the macro perspective. 

As for the "spend," I think you are being overly binary. I am not sure that the difference between OpenAI spend on cloud compute and open source model is all that different. The difference is what frontier models charge THEIR customers. THAT profit margin WILL evaporate. But the spend on compute could, very well, go up. And that is why cloud compute revenue should not be linked purely to frontier spend.

Nonetheless, every technological revolution throughout history ended in a capex boom and then bust. THAT is for CERTAIN. I am trying to navigate WHEN that happens. Because the difference between NOW and 2029 or 2030 is HUGE for investors. Just saying that it will all end in tears is not additive to anyone. EVERY capex boom has ended in tears.

It is very interesting to me how passionately people hate all things AI. It is causing many to conflate the viability (nay... validity) of frontier models with the business case for datacenters. The two are not the same. 

If anything, if frontier models "go to zero," the cost of using AI will decrease, boosting overall demand for the technology and thus increasing the need for AI capex.
